analysis.one_liner: Bans landlords from using credit checks to screen rental applicants.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced July 14, 2025 with no cosponsors, sits in the House Financial Services Committee with no action since its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act to make it illegal for landlords to pull a tenant's credit report when deciding whether to rent to them, how big a security deposit to charge, or whether to keep them as a tenant [S2]. The ban applies even if the applicant agrees to the check [S2]. The only carve-out is that a landlord who denies an application can receive a report when reconsidering that denial case by case [S2]. Today, a low credit score — often the residue of medical debt, job loss, or simply never having borrowed — can get an application rejected or saddled with a higher deposit even when the person can afford the rent [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Renters with thin or damaged credit histories. That includes young people who haven't borrowed yet, people recovering from medical debt or job loss, survivors of divorce or domestic violence whose credit was harmed, and people who pay all their bills on time in cash. They could no longer be denied an apartment, charged a bigger deposit, or graded on lease terms because of a three-digit score.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters with poor or no credit

how_it_helps.text: Bars housing providers from using any report bearing on creditworthiness, credit standing, or credit capacity when evaluating a rental application, setting the security deposit or lease terms, or deciding whether to retain a tenant [S2].
Applies the ban even when the applicant consents to the check, closing the loophole of application fees that pay for a credit pull [S2].
Allows a report only for a landlord's individualized reconsideration of a denial, giving rejected applicants a path to be re-evaluated without the score as an automatic gate [S2].
Amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act directly, so the rule would bind consumer reporting agencies and landlords nationwide through an existing federal enforcement framework [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and property owners, who lose the credit check as a quick, cheap filter for judging whether an applicant will pay rent, and would bear more of the risk of a nonpaying tenant. Credit bureaus and the tenant screening industry also lose the revenue from millions of rental screening reports each year. In exchange, landlords would presumably lean harder on other screening tools like income verification, rental history, and references.

drawbacks.text: A credit report is one of the few standardized, nationwide signals a landlord has about whether an applicant pays bills on time; without it, landlords may fall back on subjective judgments, local references that disadvantage newcomers, or higher security deposits and rent spreads for everyone to cover the added risk [S2].

The bill applies to any person who leases residential real estate to an individual, including small individual landlords, and lets no exception pass even with applicant consent, which some good-faith landlords and applicants who want to show strong credit could see as overbroad [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For renters, the benefit is real: credit scores are a poor proxy for whether someone will pay rent, and they embed past hardship — medical debt, layoffs, eviction filings that never became judgments — into a lifelong housing barrier. The cost falls on landlords, who lose a cheap default screen and take on more screening work and some added risk, which could show up as higher deposits or tighter income requirements. The honest weakness of the bill is that it removes a screen without funding or requiring any replacement, so outcomes depend on what landlords substitute.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 14, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has sat with no further action, no cosponsors, and no hearing or vote [S1][S4][S3].

narrative.text: Rep. Maxwell Frost introduced the End Tenant Credit Screening Act on July 14, 2025 [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced, and no markup, hearing, or vote appears in its action history [S4].
No other House member has signed on as a cosponsor [S3].

The bill would add a new subsection to the Fair Credit Reporting Act barring any person from procuring or using a consumer report bearing on creditworthiness for tenant screening purposes, including setting deposits, lease terms, or tenant retention [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far nobody has gained or lost — the bill has not moved, and current screening rules remain in place, benefiting landlords and the tenant screening industry by default.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords and screening firms, by default

for.name: Rep. Maxwell Frost
for.role: Sponsor; sole House sponsor, referred the bill to the House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Tenant Credit Screening Act on July 14, 2025 [S1][S4].

sides.party_line_note: No one has opposed it on the record — no committee vote, no floor action, no recorded opposition — and no Republican or other Democrat has cosponsored, so the partisan shape of the issue is not yet visible in this record [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Tenant screening and background check companies
industries.note: Rental screening reports are a core product line; the bill deletes the largest legal reason a landlord pulls credit data on an applicant. Renters would no longer be priced or rejected off a report these companies sell [S2].

Landlord pulls of credit reports are a high-volume, low-effort revenue stream, and the bureaus have marketed paid 'rent credit' programs to consumers; the ban eliminates the landlord side of that market [S2].

Landlords lose a cheap, standardized screen for payment risk and would carry more uncertainty about applicants, likely substituting income checks and deposits. Some renters they would otherwise have rejected become tenable tenants [S2].

analysis.trajectory: A first-term House bill with zero cosponsors, referred to a committee with a crowded agenda, typically goes nowhere: no hearing, no markup, and it will likely die when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027 unless it picks up cosponsors or a committee champion. Companion action in the Senate would be a prerequisite for anything further.
